summary: A working document describing the Decode-Encode Language (DEL), a machine-independent language for two network tasks: taking input from interactive consoles and packing it into messages, and unpacking incoming messages to build display information for a user. It was written at SRI and invited comments as the language evolved.

eli5.summary: It is a tiny made-up language that tells a computer how to pack a user's key presses into a parcel for the network and unpack parcels that arrive.

subtitle: A 1969 working paper on shipping small programs across the ARPA network so remote users get instant feedback.

tldr.problem: Running interactive programs across the network was expected to be the first problem faced, and different sites had different consoles and character sets.
tldr.mechanism: The server host sends a program written in DEL to the user host, which compiles it and runs it with a standard library. It translates console input into messages and incoming messages into display output.
tldr.outcome: The paper is a working document for the evolution of the language and invites comments, so it is a proposal and not a standard.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 5 as unknown, and the text itself calls it a working document for the evolution of DEL. It does not describe any later outcome.

sections.title: Where DEL Came From
sections.content:
The Decode-Encode Language (DEL), written by Jeff Rulifson, is a machine independent language for two network tasks. One is accepting input codes from interactive consoles, giving immediate feedback and packing the result into message packets. The other is accepting message packets from another computer, unpacking them, building trees of display information and sending other information to the user.

The initial ARPA network working group met at SRI on October 25-26, 1968, and agreed beforehand that running interactive programs across the network would be the first problem faced. Further meetings followed in November and December 1968, and the first public release of the paper was at the BBN NET meeting in Cambridge on February 13, 1969. The document calls itself a working document for the evolution of DEL.
sections.eli5: A group of people met and decided that the first thing computers on the network should learn was letting someone sit at one computer and use another. DEL was their idea for how to do it.

sections.title: Translators and the Universal Representation
sections.content:
The Net Standard Translator (NST) is a library of programs that meshes with code compiled at the user site from the DEL programs it receives. Its lowest level of use just passes data through in the user host's normal format. A middle level provides echo tables for a TTY: echo characters, translate them to the server host's character set, pack them and send them on break characters. The most ambitious level runs large display-oriented systems from remote consoles, where a DEL program on the user host handles immediate feedback and only sends messages at appropriate button pushes.

To limit the number of translators needed, there is a universal hardware representation. For example, a display is a square whose mid-point has coordinates (0,0) and whose range is -1 to 1 on both axes, so a point can be given to any accuracy regardless of the display's raster density.

The advantages given are that each site compiles the symbolic program into code suited to its own machine, can add or remove console features without new tables from the host, and automatically gets new host features when the host changes its program.
sections.eli5: Instead of every computer learning every other computer's quirks, they all describe things in one shared way, like drawing on a square sheet from -1 to 1.

sections.title: From Keyboard to Host and Back
sections.content:
In the user-to-host direction, the Encode program maps semi-raw input bits into a stream suited to the serving host's subsystem. The server-host subsystem supplies it in symbolic form when first requested, and it is compiled at the user machine. It may pack to break characters, map characters, translate them and give immediate feedback, which goes to local display management. Output for the server host goes through the IMP, and on the host a reception program reorders the standard packets into messages the host accepts.

In the host-to-user direction, output goes through Decode, a map similar to Encode that formats display output into a simplified logical-entity stream. The Decode program was sent to the host at the same time the Encode program went to the user machine. The user reception translator then reorders pieces and, for displays, display control puts the logical information into the user site's format. The paper suggests that a straight line should be sent as a line rather than as a series of 500 short vectors.
sections.eli5: When you press a key, a helper packs it into a parcel the other computer understands. When the other computer answers, a second helper unpacks the parcel and draws it on your screen.

sections.title: The DEL Language Itself
sections.content:
The syntax is given as meta-language rules. A program is declarations followed by procedures, and procedures may be functions (which return values), procedures (which do not) or co-routines, which have no names or arguments and start from a PIPE declaration. Declarations cover REAL and INTEGER numbers, constants, trees, pointers, buffers, labels and pipes.

The language has arithmetic and bitwise operators, conjunctive expressions with AND, OR and NOT, and conditional, loop and case statements. It also has semi-tree manipulation and message statements such as start message, append message byte and send message. Display buffers hold logical entities, with an intensity from 0 to 1 and a position register on a screen normalised from -1 to +1.

The paper is unfinished: it leaves open questions in the text, such as how global declarations are to be handled, and ends with sample program fragments and a distribution list.
sections.eli5: DEL has words for counting, making choices, repeating things, and building messages to send. It was still a draft, with some questions left open.
